title.en: Hatshepsut the Female Horus: Punt and the Garden for Amun
title.zh: 女荷魯斯哈特謝普蘇特：彭特與阿蒙之園

region.en: Deir el-Bahari, Thebes, Egypt (the queen's terraced temple and the Punt reliefs)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯代爾巴哈里（女王階台神廟與彭特浮雕）

texts.period: Reign of Hatshepsut, 18th Dynasty (c. 1479-1458 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXV, 'Amenhotep the Magnificent and Queen Tiy' (Hatshepsut section)

summary.en: The queen who reigned alone as 'the female Horus': on the walls of her terraced temple the mythical scenes of her birth were carved so she might be recognized as 'a son of the sun', depicted with her male double and wearing a false beard on state occasions; her most famous undertaking was the eight ships sent to Punt for myrrh trees and sacred animals — 'It was her pious wish that Amun should have a garden to walk in.'
summary.zh: 獨掌國柄之『女荷魯斯』：其階台神廟壁上刻其誕生之神話場景，使世人認其為『日神之子』——像旁雕其男性雙身，國典則戴假鬚；其最著之事乃遣八舟赴彭特求沒藥樹與聖獸——『其虔誠之願：使阿蒙有園可遊。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient history-legend retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The 'male double' and false beard are the queen's own royal ideology.

passages.text: After a time the usurping prince had to recognize the co-regency of Hatshepsut. But, ere long, he was thrust aside, and the queen reigned alone as 'the female Horus'.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXV.

passages.text: She completed the great mortuary temple at Der-el-Bahari, which had been begun under Thothmes II. It was modelled on the smaller temple of Mentuhotep, and is still magnificent in ruin. Situated against the western cliffs at Thebes, it was constructed in three terraces with sublime colonnades finely proportioned and exquisitely wrought. An inner chamber was excavated from the rock. On the temple walls the mythical scenes in connection with the birth of the queen were sculptured in low relief, and to get over the difficulty of being recognized as a 'son of the sun', Hatshepsut was depicted in company of her male 'double'. On state occasions she wore a false beard.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXV.

passages.text: The queen's most famous undertaking was to send an expedition of eight ships to the land of Punt to obtain myrrh trees, incense, rare woods, and sacred animals for the temple. It was her pious wish that Amun should have a garden to walk in.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXV.

passages.text: After her death no more is heard of her favourite Senmut, or her daughter, whom she had selected as her successor. Her name was ruthlessly erased from her monuments. All the indications point to a military revolt, supported by a section of the priesthood, at a time of national peril.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXV.

title.en: Ramesses at Kadesh: 'My Hand Is More to Thee Than Hundreds of Thousands'
title.zh: 拉美西斯於卡迭石：『我手勝於爾之十萬大軍』

region.en: Kadesh on the Orontes, Syria (the trap of the Hittite chariots)
region.zh: 敘利亞奧龍特斯河畔卡迭石（赫梯戰車之陷阱）

texts.period: Battle of year 5 of Ramesses II (c. 1275 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII, 'The Empire of Rameses and the Homeric Age'

summary.en: The army in four divisions named Amon, Ra, Ptah and Sutekh; the overconfident Pharaoh lured to Kadesh and surrounded with only a fragment of his force — until, as the court poet sang, he called upon Ra, and the sun god appeared before him: 'Alone thou art not, for I, thy father, am beside thee, and my hand is more to thee than hundreds of thousands. I who love the brave am the giver of victory.' The battle became the subject of temple reliefs in which Ramesses bends his bow like a giant — and the war ended in a treaty witnessed by a thousand Egyptian gods and a thousand Hittite gods.
summary.zh: 大軍分四團，即以阿蒙、拉、卜塔、蘇特克四神為名；王輕信俘言，中伏於卡迭石，幾全軍盡沒——宮廷詩人詠曰：王呼拉，日神即現其前：『爾非獨也，我父在側，我手勝於爾之十萬大軍；我愛勇者，乃勝利之賜者。』此戰遂鐫於神廟浮雕，王彎弓如巨人——戰終以和約：一千埃及神與一千赫梯神共為見證。

sensitivity.note: Ancient battle-poem retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The Kadesh 'poem' is the Ramesses II court-literature version of the battle.

passages.text: The Egyptian army was in four divisions, named Amon, Ra, Ptah, and Sutekh. Rameses was in haste to invest Kadesh, and pressed on with the Amon regiment, followed closely by the Ra regiment. The other two were, when he reached the city, at least a day's march in the rear. — The overconfident Pharaoh was being led into a trap.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII.

passages.text: Rameses had achieved a victory, but at a terrible cost. He returned to Egypt without accomplishing the capture of Kadesh, and created for himself a great military reputation by recording his feats of personal valour on temple walls and monuments. A poet who sang his praises declared that when the Pharaoh found himself surrounded, and, of course, 'alone', he called upon Ra, whereupon the sun god appeared before him and said: 'Alone thou art not, for I, thy father, am beside thee, and my hand is more to thee than hundreds of thousands. I who love the brave am the giver of victory.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.

passages.text: The treaty, which was drawn up in 1271 B.C., made reference to previous agreements, but these, unfortunately, have perished; it was signed by the two monarchs, and witnessed by a thousand Egyptian gods and a thousand Hittite gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.

title.en: Bes the Dwarf God: Music, War, and Serpents Between His Teeth
title.zh: 矮神貝斯：樂神、戰神與碎蛇者

region.en: Deir el-Bahari, Thebes, Egypt (oldest Bes image, attending the birth of Hatshepsut)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯代爾巴哈里（最古之貝斯像，侍哈特謝普蘇特誕生）

texts.period: Prominent from the 18th Dynasty, possibly 12th; oracle at Abydos into Roman times (Mackenzie 1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII, the imported and grotesque gods

summary.en: The grotesque household god from Africa: Bes the dwarf with long arms and crooked legs, cat-like ears, bushy hair and beard, wearing the skin of a wild animal with the tail trailing — a war god, a god of music playing a harp, and a love god, always drawn full face; he attends at the birth of Hatshepsut in the oldest surviving image, keeps an oracle at Abydos, and as nurse of Harpokrates guards the child god against serpents 'which he tore to pieces between his teeth.'
summary.zh: 非洲來之怪誕家宅神：貝斯矮而臂長腿曲，耳如貓、鬚髮蓬然，披獸皮曳尾——為戰神、抱琴之樂神、亦是愛神，恆以正像示人；代爾巴哈里最古之像中侍哈特謝普蘇特誕生，於阿拜多斯有神諭，又為哈波克拉特斯之乳保，護嬰神而碎蛇『於齒間』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: The grotesque god Bes also came into prominence during the Eighteenth Dynasty; it is possible that he was introduced as early as the Twelfth. Although his worship spread into Syria he appears to have been of African origin and may have been imported from Somaliland. Like the Deng, he was a dwarf with long arms and crooked legs; his nose was broad and flat, his ears projected like those of a cat, he had bushy hair and eyebrows and a beard, his lips were thick and gross. Over his back he wore the skin of a wild animal, the tail trailing behind.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII.

passages.text: He was a war god, a god of music playing a harp, and a love god. The oldest surviving representation of Bes is found in the Der el Bahari temple of Amon, where he attends at the birth of Hatshepsut. As late as Roman times he was known by his oracle at Abydos. Absorbed by the sun worshippers, he became the nurse of Harpokrates (Horus) whom he nourished and amused. He also guarded the child god against the attacks of serpents, which he tore to pieces between his teeth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.

title.en: The Imported Goddesses: Astarte, Lady of Horses, and Kadesh the Holy One
title.zh: 外來女神：馭馬者阿斯塔特與『聖者』卡迭石

region.en: Memphis and Tanis, Egypt (temples of the imported love-and-war goddesses)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯與塔尼斯（外來愛與戰女神之廟）

texts.period: Imported during the 18th Dynasty wars with Syria (c. 1450-1300 BCE); retold in Mackenzie 1913

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII, the foreign elements in the Egyptian religion

summary.en: The empire brought Asiatic goddesses up the Nile: Astarte, 'introduced into the Nile valley with the horse', a lunar deity and goddess of war with the head of a lioness — as the 'Lady of Horses' she stands in a chariot driving four horses over a fallen foe; Kadesh 'the holy one', another form of Astarte, the moon goddess nude on the back of a lioness carrying lotus flowers and two serpents — and Baal was worshipped at Tanis, where a temple of the 'strange Aphrodite' stood in Herodotus' day.
summary.zh: 帝國時代異邦女神沿尼羅而上：阿斯塔特『隨馬而入埃及』，為月神與戰神，獅首——稱『馭馬之主』，立於戰車驅四馬踏倒敵者；『聖者』卡迭石為其別形，裸身立於獅背，一手持蓮與鏡，一手持雙蛇；坦尼斯則奉巴阿爾——希羅多斯所見之『異邦阿佛洛狄忒』小廟即在孟菲斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient syncretism retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Astarte was worshipped in Egypt early in the Eighteenth Dynasty, and was a lunar deity and goddess of war. She appears to have been introduced into the Nile valley with the horse. Like Tefnut, and other Egyptian feline goddesses, she was depicted with the head of a lioness. As the 'Lady of Horses' she stands in a chariot driving four horses over a fallen foe.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXVII.

passages.text: Kadesh (Quedesh) 'the holy one', was another form of Astarte. As the 'mistress of all the gods', and the patroness of the 'unmoral' women connected with her temples, she emphasized the licentious phase of the character of Ashtoreth... The Egyptians depicted her as a moon goddess, standing nude on the back of a lioness, which indicated that she was imported from the Hittites; in one hand she carries lotus flowers and what appears to be a mirror, and in the other two serpents. As 'the eye of Ra' she links with Hathor and Sekhet.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.

passages.text: At Memphis she was adored with the moon god Ah, and when Herodotus visited the city he found a small temple dedicated to 'the strange Aphrodite' (Venus). She was the goddess of the eastern part of Tanis (Zoan).
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXVII.
